source: Voter Freedom channel, 97 catalog videos; transcripts from data/generated/transcripts.json (88 with text). Each script adapts one video for a Question 3 volunteer read: first person, hook under 12 words, about 25 seconds, closing on the ask. A number appears in a script only if the source transcript carries it; `number` names the figure kept. Many source transcripts are machine-translated back into English; wording is cleaned, claims are not extended. Written 2026-10-21.

scripts.title: Why Millions of Independent Voters Are Locked Out
scripts.hook: The biggest hidden problem in our politics.
scripts.text: Here is the biggest hidden problem in our politics. Forty-seven percent of voters now call themselves independent — more than both parties combined — yet in sixteen states millions of them are shut out of the primaries their taxes pay for. And where districts run safely one color, the primary is the real election. Question 3 opens ours to every voter. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Kept the source's two figures and its premise; the ask is ours.

scripts.title: Taxation Without Choice
scripts.hook: These are our taxes paying for these ballots.
scripts.text: Look — our taxes pay for the ballots, the polling places, the voting machines. But as an independent in a closed primary, I'm told: pick a party or stand aside. That is taxation without choice. The fix is simple. Open the primary. Let the voters in. Question 3 does exactly that in Massachusetts. Vote yes on Question 3. That's all I have to say.
scripts.note: Source's own argument and cadence, cleaned of translation artifacts.

scripts.title: What Does It Mean To Be Independent?
scripts.hook: More of us are done with both parties.
scripts.text: More and more of us, especially younger voters, call ourselves independent — fed up with both parties. We watch enormous elections, billions spent, and little change. That isn't apathy; it's a verdict on the menu. Question 3 puts every candidate in front of every voter in one open primary, so an independent's vote counts from the start. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Trend claim kept general, as the source states it; no figure in source.

scripts.title: When Primaries Shape the Outcome
scripts.hook: Ninety percent of seats, chosen by ten percent of voters.
scripts.text: Nationally, close to ninety percent of House seats are decided by roughly the ten percent of voters who show up for party primaries — the most ideological slice of the electorate. That is how the pendulum swings so hard every four years. Question 3 opens the first round to everyone, so the middle finally counts. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's statistic, attributed nationally as the source gives it.

scripts.title: Why Nothing Passes
scripts.hook: They aren't afraid of you.
scripts.text: Ever wonder how politicians walk away from unfinished work? It isn't laziness — it's fear. Not of you; of party insiders. Work across the aisle and a low-turnout primary ends your career. Closed primaries punish the job being done. Question 3 takes that leverage away: one open primary, every voter, top two advance. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's mechanism argument, intact.

scripts.title: It's Fundamentally Broken
scripts.hook: You shouldn't have to join a club to vote.
scripts.text: I registered independent, then learned I'd have to join a party just to vote in the election that matters. That is un-American. No private organization should hold a legal privilege over your constitutional right to vote — you already pay for these elections with your taxes. Question 3 opens the primary to every voter in Massachusetts. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The speaker's club argument, generalized; the Alaska aside dropped (its system differs from Q3).

scripts.title: Name Another Job...
scripts.hook: Name another job with a thirteen percent rating.
scripts.text: Name another job where a thirteen percent rating keeps you employed forever. A surgeon loses the license. A contractor ends up in court. Congress gets re-elected — because November is settled months earlier, in low-turnout primaries where insiders pick winners. They made your disappointment free of charge. Question 3 reopens the contest: every voter, one primary, top two. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Kept the source's 13% framing and its 90% claim; sharpened, not extended.

scripts.title: You Served, But You Can't Vote?
scripts.hook: I voted from a tent overseas. Now I'm locked out.
scripts.text: I mailed ballots home from a tent overseas and hoped they'd arrive. Voting is one of the rights I served for. Most young veterans after 9/11 — about 55 percent — are independents, and in fifteen states with closed primaries we get no say in the round that decides ninety percent of winners. Question 3 opens that round here. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.number: 55% of post-9/11 veterans independent; ~90% decided in the first round
scripts.note: The veteran's own account and figures.

scripts.title: Let Every Voter In
scripts.hook: A candidate can win with ten percent.
scripts.text: In a closed party primary, a candidate can win with ten percent of the vote — playing to the loudest wing of one party, while independents wait outside. That's wrong. In an open primary, every candidate stands on one ballot before every voter, and winning means persuading the whole district. Massachusetts can choose that system. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's Pennsylvania framing generalized; its figure kept.

scripts.title: We Need Better Ideas
scripts.hook: Eight percent of voters decide ninety percent of races.
scripts.text: Here's an idea: no taxpayer-funded primary unless every voter can vote in it. Today about eight percent of voters determine the outcome of ninety percent of congressional races — and division becomes a survival strategy, because the system rewards it. Systems built to encourage division can be rebuilt to encourage cooperation. Question 3 is that rebuild for Massachusetts. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The source's own proposal and arithmetic.

scripts.title: Independents Deserve A Voice
scripts.hook: I left the party. They kept my ballot.
scripts.text: When I left my party, I didn't realize I was signing away my vote. My husband's ballot arrived in the mail; mine never came. The election office told me: no party, no primary ballot. I'm the same taxpayer, the same citizen, the same voter. Leaving a party should never cost you the election that matters most. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Her story, first person, with the ask added.

scripts.title: The Incentives Are Broken
scripts.hook: Forty trillion in debt, and nobody cooperates.
scripts.text: We just passed forty trillion dollars in national debt, and our leaders still can't work together. Why? Because they're always looking over their shoulder at the next party primary instead of at the majority they serve. The dysfunction isn't a character flaw — it's an incentive structure. Question 3 changes the incentive: win the whole electorate, not a faction. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's connection of debt to primary incentives, kept as its argument.

scripts.title: Wait…They Actually Work Together?
scripts.hook: They couldn't share dinner. Now they write bills together.
scripts.text: Democrats and Republicans who couldn't share a dinner table are writing bills together where primaries are open. The reason is simple: when everyone votes in the first round, candidates have to talk to people outside their base — including independents, the fastest-growing group of voters. It isn't a cure-all. It's oxygen. Question 3 brings it to Massachusetts. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's claim kept qualitative, including its own 'not a panacea' caveat.

scripts.title: Vote Beyond Party
scripts.hook: Ever heard of an open primary?
scripts.text: Ever heard of an open primary? It means you don't vote a Republican ballot or a Democratic ballot — you just vote for the person you think is best, whoever they are. One ballot, every candidate, every voter. That's the whole idea, and it's on our ballot as Question 3. If that sounds productive for democracy — it is. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The street-interview explanation, kept conversational.

scripts.title: Fix The System, Change The Politics
scripts.hook: The election model decides the politicians you get.
scripts.text: The way we run elections decides which candidates run and which ones win. We keep blaming individuals and ignoring the system around them. People are overrated; system design is underrated. Massachusetts gets one design decision this fall: keep the closed first round, or open it to every voter and candidate. Question 3 is the redesign. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The source's systems-over-people thesis; its catalogue of other models dropped (Q3 is top-two).

scripts.title: Running To The Extremes
scripts.hook: Forty-five percent independent — and still no say.
scripts.text: Some forty-five percent of Americans now call themselves independent. They say they want a sensible middle, yet politics keeps running to the extremes. There's a structural reason: in most races, independents can't vote in the primary that decides everything, and neither party wants to change that — it would loosen their grip. Question 3 changes it here. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Kept the structural claim; dropped the source's celebrity speculation.

scripts.title: Rocky Steps vs National Debt
scripts.hook: Twenty-three million voters, completely shut out.
scripts.text: Why don't we elect people who deal with the cost of living, housing, health care? Because of how we elect them. Forty-seven percent of voters are independent — more than either party — yet closed primaries in sixteen states shut out twenty-three million of them entirely. Open primaries put every candidate before every voter. Massachusetts votes on exactly that. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The stunt framing dropped; its figures and argument kept.

scripts.title: Alaska Has A Better Way To Vote
scripts.hook: Alaska opened its primary. Turnout jumped.
scripts.text: Alaska gave every voter the same primary ballot, whatever their party. In 2024 its primary turnout hit 37 percent — third-highest in the country, against a national average around 21. Their version advances four and ranks them; Question 3 here advances the top two — but the open door is the same door. More voters, less fear, leaders who answer to a real majority. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The mechanical difference from Q3 is stated in the script itself.

scripts.title: Alaska Gets Things Done
scripts.hook: Votes cast in real races rose sixty percent.
scripts.text: After Alaska opened its primary in 2020, ballots cast in competitive races rose by nearly sixty percent, and both legislative chambers ended up run by problem-solving coalitions rather than one party. Their system advances four; ours would advance two. The lesson travels either way: answer to the whole electorate and the work gets done. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.number: ~60% rise in ballots cast in competitive races
scripts.note: Outcome claims kept with the system difference stated.

scripts.title: Independents Are On The Rise In America
scripts.hook: Forty-seven percent of us belong to no party.
scripts.text: Forty-seven percent of Americans now identify as independent — the highest in over a decade of polling, more than either party, and a majority of adults under forty-five. That's the electorate we actually have. Our primary system was built for a different one. Question 3 updates Massachusetts: one open primary where every one of us votes. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The poll's figures, attributed as polling.

scripts.title: Our Republic for the Next 250 Years
scripts.hook: The cradle of democracy locks out a million voters.
scripts.text: We're 250 years into the idea that power comes from the people. Yet in Pennsylvania — the Constitution's birthplace — about 1.4 million voters are excluded from primaries for being independent. Massachusetts shouldn't celebrate the founders by keeping their descendants out of the vote. Question 3 lets everyone vote in every election. For the next 250 years, vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Pennsylvania figure kept attributed to Pennsylvania; the bridge to Q3 is the adaptation.

scripts.title: Independents Are Locked Out
scripts.hook: Thirty-nine million Americans, told to join or be silent.
scripts.text: "Are you going to vote?" "I can't — I'm independent." "You could register with a party." I could. I won't. There are more than 39 million Americans registered with no party, and over twenty states keep primaries closed or half-closed to them. Choosing who represents us shouldn't require joining anyone's club. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.number: 39 million unaffiliated; 20+ states closed or partially closed
scripts.note: The phone-call story kept verbatim in spirit; figures are the source's.

scripts.title: Millions of Independent Voters Are Shut Out
scripts.hook: By November, it's already over.
scripts.text: The fastest-growing political force in the country is people who join neither party. And they can't vote until November — when over 92 percent of congressional districts aren't competitive anymore. The real decision already happened, without them. If you believe in democracy, you let people in at the start. Question 3 opens the start. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's figure and argument.

scripts.title: Over Before Your Vote
scripts.hook: A million voters, waiting for an election that's over.
scripts.text: In Maryland, about a million voters — roughly 22 percent — are independent, and the primaries are still closed to them. Fewer than ten percent of congressional races are competitive by November, so independents vote after the outcome is settled. Many give in and register with a party they don't believe in. Massachusetts can skip that bargain. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Maryland figures attributed to Maryland.

scripts.title: Crowning Congress
scripts.hook: One hundred fifty seats won without a single vote.
scripts.text: Here's the headline nobody ran: 150 congressional candidates effectively won before a single vote — no primary challenger, no real general election. More than one in three members, crowned rather than chosen. Americans deserve competition, not coronations, and the fix is the primary system itself: open it, let the leaders advance, let the majority decide. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.number: 150 candidates; more than one in three members
scripts.note: Source's own headline and remedy.

scripts.title: Ballots In Name Only
scripts.hook: A menu with one dish isn't a menu.
scripts.text: Thirty-two states will hold 2026 elections without one competitive congressional district. Sixty percent of state legislative seats will go uncontested from primary through November. It's a restaurant with one dish on the menu — then blaming the diners for not loving it. A ballot you can't change anything with is a ballot in name only. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Kept the source's figures and its restaurant comparison.

scripts.title: The Primary Is the Whole Ballgame
scripts.hook: Eighty-three percent of districts are decided in the primary.
scripts.text: Eighty-three percent of congressional districts are decided in the primary — the primary is the whole ballgame. People ask, why not just register with the dominant party? Because no one should have to join a private organization to have a voice in a public election. The parties can nominate whoever they like; the election belongs to the voters. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's figure and its club argument.

scripts.title: We Need more Competition
scripts.hook: Everywhere else, we compete. In politics, two choices.
scripts.text: In everything else we do, we compete. In politics there are two choices, and in a safe seat, none. A politician who can't lose has no reason to work for you. Open the primary and the ballot carries more than two real contenders — suddenly solving your problems is the job again. Competition is the point. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The competition argument, cleaned.

scripts.title: A Healthy Democracy
scripts.hook: This is a gift to the parties, honestly.
scripts.text: Open primaries help democracy, period. With this many Americans dissatisfied — including people still inside both parties — anything that adds choice, voice, and flexibility is worth having. This isn't about eliminating the parties; honestly, it's a gift that helps them save themselves from themselves. Flexibility is health. Massachusetts can choose it this fall. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Kept the source's framing, including the 'gift to the parties' line; dropped its closing joke.

scripts.title: The Case for Open Primaries
scripts.hook: Don't wait until November. It's already decided.
scripts.text: The public hasn't caught on: the decisions happen in the primaries. Districts are drawn so that ninety to ninety-three percent of members of Congress face only one real election — their primary — and the rules of that election exclude independents. These are public elections, publicly funded. Let every voter vote in them. Stop waiting for November. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's figures and its 'wait until November' culture point.

scripts.title: Closed Primaries Undermine Election Integrity
scripts.hook: You want election integrity? Start with the primary.
scripts.text: Everyone talks about election integrity. Here's an integrity problem hiding in plain sight: a closed primary lets a narrow circle choose the two names everyone else gets. Independents never touch it. The winners answer to a wing, not a district — and when I take the oath, the oath is to every person in the district. Open the first round. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: A former member's argument, first person as in the source.

scripts.title: What's the Impact of Gerrymandering?
scripts.hook: Ninety percent of races end before November.
scripts.text: The quiet scandal of gerrymandering, in red states and blue: by November roughly ninety percent of congressional races are already decided. The primary is the only election that matters. California has run an open, nonpartisan first round for sixteen years and leads the nation in primary turnout — over forty percent. Public elections, publicly funded, open to the public. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: California's experience as the source states it.

scripts.title: Closed Primaries Vs Open Primaries
scripts.hook: Seven percent of voters chose eighty-seven percent of Congress.
scripts.text: In 2024, seven percent of voters effectively elected eighty-seven percent of Congress — that's the closed-primary math. One study compared states on fourteen quality-of-life measures: states with all-candidate primaries did better on nine and worse on none. That doesn't prove the ballot did it alone, but it says opening the door doesn't hurt — and likely helps. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Kept the study's own causality caveat, as the source did.

scripts.title: It Starts With Open Primaries
scripts.hook: Ask anyone: want to vote for anyone, any election?
scripts.text: Ask the average American: would you like to vote for any candidate, from any party, in every election? Of course. We pay for the primaries — the workers, the ballots, all of it — while a huge share of us can't participate. And when someone says this is too complicated for you, ask why they'd rather you not look. They're holding power. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The veteran's argument with the names dropped.

scripts.title: Two Private Clubs
scripts.hook: Our democracy is run by two private clubs.
scripts.text: Our democracy is run by two private clubs, and neither solves enough problems to deserve special legal privileges. Forcing voters to pick the lesser of two evils, again and again, is control — not representation. One open primary for every race puts every candidate on level ground and makes every voice equally loud. That sounds like freedom to me. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's club framing and its 'sounds like freedom' close.

scripts.title: The Primary Problem
scripts.hook: The biggest solvable problem in our politics.
scripts.text: Party primaries are the biggest solvable problem in American politics. They disenfranchise millions — independents are barred outright in nearly two dozen states — and they're fixable at the state level, which is exactly where we are. States are already moving; the reform is pragmatic, not radical. Massachusetts' turn is on this ballot. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.number: nearly two dozen states bar independents
scripts.note: The author's thesis, compressed.

scripts.title: The Rise of Independent Voters
scripts.hook: Ten thousand Americans a week leave the parties.
scripts.text: Every week, about ten thousand Americans change their registration from Democrat or Republican to independent. They're now 48 percent of the country — the fastest-growing part of the electorate — and our election system still treats them like uninvited guests. Many have moral objections to joining an organization they don't support. They shouldn't have to. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's figures and its 'uninvited guests' image.

scripts.title: Frustrated with Politics?
scripts.hook: It's just math: the extremes are the majority.
scripts.text: If our politics makes you angry, look at the incentives. When primaries decide ninety percent of elections and only five to ten percent of the electorate votes in them, fifty-one percent of that sliver is a majority — and it's always the most extreme sliver. The fix is letting everyone vote from the start. More voters in, more representative results out. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The source's arithmetic; its ranked-choice clause omitted — Question 3 is the open-primary half.

scripts.title: No Football For You
scripts.hook: Imagine declaring team loyalty just to watch football.
scripts.text: Imagine the league announcing: only fans who declared a team before the season may watch the playoffs. Ridiculous — and it's how our elections work. The real contest is the primary, months before November, and in sixteen states independents are locked outside the stadium. In 2024, seven percent of voters elected 87 percent of Congress. One ballot, every candidate, every voter. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The source's own football analogy, condensed.

scripts.title: Is Congress Performing Instead Of Governing?
scripts.hook: Eighty-six percent of us disapprove. Nothing changes.
scripts.text: Congress gets more theatrical every year — chasing clips instead of writing laws — and 86 percent of Americans disapprove. Nothing changes, because the system rewards the performance: win a narrow primary, keep the seat. In an open primary I'd have to earn votes across the whole district, because the oath is to the whole district. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: A former member's point, first person as spoken.

scripts.title: A Warning from George Washington
scripts.hook: Washington's farewell warned us about exactly this.
scripts.text: George Washington's farewell address warned against faction — the group becoming more important than the people. Today a third of some states' voters register independent, and the system tells them they're less equal: join a private club or skip the primary your taxes fund. An open primary is the people's primary. Heed the oldest warning we have. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.number: about a third registered independent (Iowa, per source)
scripts.note: Washington's warning as the source frames it; Iowa figure generalized with attribution here.

scripts.title: The Real Story: 93% Didn't Vote
scripts.hook: Ninety-three percent didn't vote. That's the story.
scripts.text: After a big-city primary, everyone argued about what the result meant. Here's what it meant: seven percent of eligible voters voted. Ninety-three percent didn't. You can't read a mandate in a turnout like that — you can only read a system that convinced people their vote doesn't matter. Open primaries are how you invite them back. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The New York specifics generalized; the figures kept.

scripts.title: A Win For Independents In DC
scripts.hook: Eighty-five thousand voters just got their ballots back.
scripts.text: Washington, D.C. just funded open primaries — 85,000 independent voters who used to be turned away will finally vote in the election that decides their city. What changed minds? Neighbors, telling neighbors they'd been locked out. This reform is moving city by city, state by state. Massachusetts is next on the ballot. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The news story as momentum, figures kept.

scripts.title: Open The Primaries
scripts.hook: New York lost three hundred thousand Democrats.
scripts.text: New York runs fully closed primaries — and lost three hundred thousand registered Democrats, most of them to independence. The party kept control and lost the voters; the loudest wings captured what remained. That's where closed systems end up. Make the winner earn a real majority of a real electorate. Open the primaries. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The source's New York account, attributed.

scripts.title: Who Speaks For New York?
scripts.hook: Thirty-seven thousand votes decided seven hundred fifty thousand people's seat.
scripts.text: Do the math on one city district: 750,000 residents, about 450,000 registered voters — and 37,000 primary votes effectively chose the winner, because the general election was a formality. Nobody can tell you what that district actually wants; most of it never got a meaningful vote. That's not representation, it's rounding error. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The arithmetic kept exactly; candidate names dropped.

scripts.title: Independent Voters in Colorado
scripts.hook: Over half of us belong to no party.
scripts.text: Here's something about my state: more than half the voters identify with neither party — yet on primary day each of us must pick one party's ballot to participate at all. There's a better way. All candidates on one ballot, every voter choosing freely across every race. More choice for voters, and candidates who must talk to everyone. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Colorado attribution kept; the mechanism described is the open ballot Q3 shares.

scripts.title: Closed Primaries are Anti-Free Market
scripts.hook: Closed primaries are as anti-free-market as it gets.
scripts.text: Closed primaries are anti-free-market and anti-American. A small, hard-core group picks the two names the rest of us choose between — and independents never touch the process. When I served, my oath was to every person in the district, so why keep a system that rewards representing a fraction? Open competition works in markets. It works in elections. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: A five-term member's free-market case, cleaned of the music tags.

scripts.title: New York’s Closed Primary
scripts.hook: The election is in my kids' school. I can't vote in it.
scripts.text: The polls are two blocks away, in my kids' public school — public workers, public machines, public money. And I can't vote there, because I'm independent. Veterans who bled for this country are told the same. We're not politically homeless; we're free — and we pay for this election. Being free shouldn't cost you your vote. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The veteran's story kept; the sports opener dropped.

scripts.title: A Win In New Mexico
scripts.hook: Three hundred forty thousand voters just got in.
scripts.text: New Mexico counted more than 340,000 registered independents who couldn't vote in primaries — then passed a law and started letting them in. The argument that won: represent your district, not the three percent of your party who already vote for you. There's a place in democracy for people who won't pick a team. Massachusetts can prove it too. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The legislative win as momentum; figures kept.

scripts.title: Not Party Driven
scripts.hook: We're not party people. Now the ballot agrees.
scripts.text: Before, the parties decided whose name you'd see — whether you agreed with them or not. Since the primary opened, the party label matters less, and that suits us: a lot of us aren't party-driven. We want the freedom to pick on values, race by race. That's the whole promise of an open ballot, and it's on ours this fall. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: An Alaskan voter's read on power shifting; ranking mechanics not invoked.

scripts.title: More Than Two Choices?
scripts.hook: Imagine the candy bucket held exactly two options.
scripts.text: At our house there's a candy bucket — some favorites, some I skip, but the options are there. Voting should feel like that: look in, see who speaks to your values, knowing your neighbors will pick differently. Wouldn't it be sad if the bucket only ever held two bars, picked by someone else? An open primary refills the bucket. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The parent's own analogy, kept whole.

scripts.title: Closed Primaries = Political Gridlock
scripts.hook: Storm Normandy, register independent, lose your vote.
scripts.text: You could be a 98-year-old veteran who stormed Normandy and, in half the states, registering independent means you're told you're not welcome in half the elections. It corrodes the House floor too: members vote no while hoping yes, because only 18 percent of Americans vote in primaries and they answer to that sliver. Open the first round. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.number: half the states closed; 18% vote in primaries
scripts.note: A sitting member's argument, figures kept.

scripts.title: Closed Primaries Fuel Extremes
scripts.hook: Organized extremes versus a disorganized majority.
scripts.text: This country has organized extremes, organized special interests, and a frustrated, disorganized majority. For most officials there's one moment they can lose power: the primary. Cross the aisle once, help the majority once, and a closed primary is where you pay for it. That risk is the whole problem — and it's removable. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The incentive diagnosis, verbatim in substance.

scripts.title: Let All Americans Vote
scripts.hook: Three million New Yorkers, effectively disenfranchised.
scripts.text: If the anger in our politics frustrates you, look at the incentive structure. Partisan primaries decide ninety percent of elections and five to ten percent of the electorate controls them — while three million independent New Yorkers are effectively shut out. Let everybody vote and you get representative turnout, representative results, and politicians rewarded for solving problems. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Figures kept with New York attribution; the ranked-choice clause omitted.

scripts.title: Locked Out Of Voting?
scripts.hook: Raise the bar for what patriotism means.
scripts.text: We're celebrating 250 years of self-government, so raise the bar on patriotism: it isn't just saluting — it's fighting for the full, equal participation of people you disagree with. Over half of military veterans identify as independent, and in state after state they can't vote in the primary their taxes fund. Fight for them. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The patriotism reframe and the veterans figure.

scripts.title: Stop Shutting Voters Out
scripts.hook: The people's primary, not the parties'.
scripts.text: Right now we literally tell independent voters: you are less equal — sign with a private club before you may vote. An open primary is the people's primary: no private organization spending tax dollars on an election for members only, every eligible citizen welcome. Do that, and suddenly an elected official has a reason to solve everyone's problems. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The Iowa framing generalized; 'people's primary' kept.

scripts.title: Primaries Are Broken
scripts.hook: Promise cooperation, lose the primary. That's the system.
scripts.text: Here's the incentive structure we built: promise to work with everybody and you lose the primary; promise war on the other side and you may well win it. Primary voters aren't even happy with their own party — they just hate the other one more. No wonder governing feels impossible. Change the incentive, change the behavior. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The political scientist's argument, minus its graphic flourish.

scripts.title: Voters Shut Out
scripts.hook: They perform for a fraction, then represent everyone.
scripts.text: Members of Congress describe their own elections to me as performances — entertaining the fraction of their party that votes in the primary. Then they win, and suddenly must represent everyone, including the half they spent a year ostracizing. Our state ran open primaries for decades: you courted every voter you'd represent. People died for this democracy. It deserves better theater. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: First-person congressional account, kept.

scripts.title: Is Democracy Ready For AI?
scripts.hook: The biggest decisions ahead, the least competitive Congress.
scripts.text: The decisions coming — about technology, the economy, security — need a Congress that works. Ours can't, and not only because of partisanship: without competitive elections we get career politicians a quarter of whom are past retirement age, asking the wrong questions at the hearings that matter. Opening primaries to all voters, including the independents locked out in sixteen states, is the most solvable fix. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.number: 16 states; a quarter past retirement age
scripts.note: The AI framing kept general; the mockery dropped.

scripts.title: Independents Pay The Price
scripts.hook: A poll tax, paid in party membership.
scripts.text: You're telling me the only way into a taxpayer-funded election is joining a private club? As an independent, I call that a poll tax — paid in membership instead of money. There's real doubt it squares with state constitutions that protect voters even more strongly than the federal one. Legislatures are starting to fix it. Massachusetts can fix it directly. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The poll-tax framing, kept as the speaker's claim.

scripts.title: We Have A Problem
scripts.hook: Eighty-three percent decided, ten percent deciding.
scripts.text: A report called it the primary problem: 83 percent of congressional seats are effectively decided in the primary, because the districts lean so hard one way. And how many Americans voted in the primaries that offered any real choice? Ten percent. A small, unrepresentative slice is choosing almost everything. It's the biggest solvable problem in our democracy. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The report's figures as the source cites them.

scripts.title: More Choices. Better Competition.
scripts.hook: Top two advance — whoever they are.
scripts.text: In an open primary the top two advance, whatever their party. Some years that's one of each; some years it's two of the same — which just means one side needs to get its act together and earn it. That's the honest version of competition: nobody's guaranteed a lane, everybody has to persuade. Massachusetts can have it. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The banter distilled to its honest-competition point.

scripts.title: Taxation Without Representation?
scripts.hook: We fought a revolution over exactly this.
scripts.text: I'm independent, and I pay for elections I'm not allowed to vote in. We fought a revolution over taxation without representation — and here it is again, politely administered. Almost half of Americans are independents now. If two companies lost half their customers, we'd call it failure; in politics we call it the system. Fair would be letting everyone in. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: Source's revolution framing and market comparison.

scripts.title: We Can Reach The Moon
scripts.hook: We can reach the moon. We can't pass a budget.
scripts.text: We're sending humans back toward the moon — proof of what this country does when it works together. Back on Earth, a shutdown left tens of thousands of workers six weeks without pay because Congress couldn't fund its own government. The difference isn't talent; it's incentives. Fixing them doesn't take rocket science — it takes opening our elections. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The contrast kept; specific program names trimmed.

scripts.title: What's The Real Story?
scripts.hook: The least competitive election of our lifetime.
scripts.text: The results nobody covered: fewer than ten percent of voters chose about ninety percent of the House. A million and a half independents were turned away from taxpayer-funded primaries. A hundred and fifty candidates won with no opponent at all. When leaders don't have to earn your vote, they don't have to deliver for you. Competition, not coronation. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The source's own summary of the 2026 primaries.

scripts.title: Who's In Charge?
scripts.hook: Ninety percent of seats: foregone conclusions.
scripts.text: Why doesn't Congress plan for the biggest changes coming at us? Because it isn't paid to. Members are paid — in the only currency that matters, re-election — to win low-turnout party primaries. By this November, ninety percent of seats will already be decided; in many districts, getting your name on the ballot is the whole job. Change what the job rewards. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The incentives argument with the celebrity reference removed.

scripts.title: OPEN vs CLOSED
scripts.hook: The real divide isn't left versus right.
scripts.text: The old left-right line explains less and less. The real divide is open versus closed. A closed system builds a wall between an institution and the people it serves: wrong party? Too bad — the system wasn't built for you. Every American knows what an open door means. Our elections should be one. Tear the wall down. Vote yes on Question 3.
scripts.note: The open/closed thesis, kept rhetorical as the source is.
